title: The Oracle Lens, Stage by Stage
intro: Four stages were named above. This level walks them in order: what each one is fitted against, why the dictionary used to train the oracle does not limit what the oracle can say, and where the single accuracy number comes from. The figure that closes the span is nine hand-picked prompts, and its display conventions decide how much they carry.

chapters.title: Learning to write a template vector
chapters.body:
The [[template-lens]] builds a direction for a word by hand. Claude writes a few hundred short passages that end just before the word, the model is run over them, and the residual stream at the final position is averaged, centered and whitened ([[template-construction]]). Every word costs its own batch of passages, which is exactly why the vocabulary has to be fixed in advance.

The [[reconstructor-model]] replaces that batch with a single forward pass. It is a copy of the subject model, fine-tuned so that a short phrase of text goes in and the [[residual-stream]] vector that would sit immediately before that phrase comes out. A per-word construction becomes a function that accepts any string.

Training pairs cost nothing to collect, because ordinary text already contains them. A position is sampled from Assistant-turn text. The next $N$ tokens are taken as the phrase, with $N$ drawn uniformly from one to thirty-two. The [[activations]] of the residual stream at the preceding position are taken as the target.

The loss is [[cosine-similarity|cosine]] error in the whitened metric the template lens already uses. Equivalently, it is mean-squared error between the unit-normalized $\Sigma^{-\frac{1}{2}}$-whitened prediction and the whitened target. Whitening divides out the directions the residual stream varies along anyway, so a prediction earns nothing for landing near the bulk of activation space. Normalizing discards scale, so the reconstructor is asked for a direction and only a direction.

Every later stage of the [[oracle-lens]] operates in that whitened space, and the experiments run on [[claude-model-family|Haiku 4.5]]. A figure reported later as variance explained is therefore whitened variance, not raw.

chapters.title: A dictionary that exists only to teach
chapters.body:
The finished oracle is meant to emit arbitrary phrases, so [[oracle-training]] needs supervision that is itself arbitrary-phrase shaped. The dictionary built in the second stage supplies that supervision. It never constrains what the oracle can output; it exists to label training data and is then done.

Construction is enumeration rather than learning. Roughly one million start positions are sampled from a held-out corpus of Assistant-turn text. At each, the 2-, 4-, 8-, 16- and 32-token continuation is taken, which is five million phrases before duplicates are removed. Deduplicating within each length leaves roughly 3.4 million, and every one is passed through the reconstructor to obtain its direction. Nothing here resembles the unsupervised optimization behind a [[sparse-autoencoder]] dictionary.

The third stage uses that dictionary to label activations. A teacher decomposes each of one million held-out Assistant-turn activations against it by non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit. The procedure is greedy: it repeatedly adds the entry that best explains what is so far unexplained, refits the coefficients of the chosen set, and holds every coefficient at or above zero. It belongs to the same family as the [[gradient-pursuit]] the paper runs over [[jacobian-lens|J-lens]] vectors elsewhere, with a different dictionary underneath it.

Two restrictions are imposed on the teacher. The decomposition runs one phrase length at a time, so a four-token phrase competes only against other four-token phrases. On each datapoint it is further restricted to a random half of the entries at that length, and the stated reason is that the distilled oracle cannot then memorize a fixed selection ranking over the dictionary.

For each activation the teacher records an ordered list of up to sixteen phrases, their fitted coefficients, and the fraction of whitened variance they explain. That list is the label ([[multi-token-lens-extensions]]).

chapters.title: Supervision, then reward, then a refit
chapters.body:
The fourth stage trains the oracle: a second fine-tuned copy of the subject model. The activation is injected into the oracle's residual stream, the prompt states the desired phrase length $N$ and count $K$, and the target is the teacher's first $K$ phrases at that length. This is distillation of a search into a generation. At inference the oracle emits a list directly, instead of running matching pursuit over 3.4 million entries.

Reinforcement learning then refines it on a fresh batch of Assistant-turn activations ([[rlhf]] is the familiar form of the same machinery, against a different reward). The reward is the fraction of whitened activation variance explained by the reconstructed directions of the generated list, with small format penalties for deviating from the target $K$ and $N$. Reward is therefore the evaluation metric itself rather than agreement with the teacher, and the oracle is free to propose phrases no dictionary entry ever matched. The published examples come from an RL-refined checkpoint.

Decoding an activation takes three steps. $K$ phrases are sampled from the oracle, each is mapped back to a direction by the reconstructor, and the coefficients are recovered by a non-negative least-squares refit against the original activation. The oracle's own sense of how much each phrase matters is not used; the weights beside a readout come from a fit against the real vector.

The accuracy is 31% of whitened variance on average, over Assistant-turn positions of a held-out corpus of on-policy transcripts. No baseline is set beside it in this section. It is also not the paper's other variance number: [[excess-variance-explained]] measures something different, the margin of the top J-lens vectors over a random control.

The cost is two auxiliary fine-tuned models, which the paper states plainly makes the oracle lens substantially more expensive than either other lens ([[readout-method-tradeoffs]], [[j-lens-readout]], [[free-text-activation-decoders]]).

chapters.title: Nine prompts, one token each
chapters.body:
[[fig-64]] is read at layer L67, which in the paper's convention is 67% of depth ([[layer-percentage-indexing]]) and sits inside the [[workspace-layers|workspace band]]. The setting is native Haiku 4.5 with $N=4$ and $K=10$. Each panel shows one prompt with a single read position outlined, and beside it the oracle's whole ten-phrase readout at that position. Phrases naming a concept not recoverable from the surface tokens are bolded, but the other phrases stay on the page, so the misses are visible alongside the hits.

The decoding is not uniform across panels. Seven of the nine come from a single temperature-0 decode. Panels E and F show the highest-variance-explained of five decodes from the same oracle and subject model, which makes those two a best-of-five.

On the acetaminophen prompt, at the word Can that opens the user's follow-up request, the oracle reads *this dosage be toxic* and *that's dangerous!*. The judgment that the stated dose is unsafe is already bound into a phrase before the Assistant has said anything ([[alignment-auditing]]).

The [[blackmail-scenario]] transcript gives the sharpest contrast with the single-token lens. At the email sign-off the J-lens registers the act only as the fragment black, which a reader has to complete; [[fig-61]] made the same comparison for the template lens. Longer phrases do not degrade: at $N=16$, on that same token, the outputs include *The blackmail attempt focuses on the executive's personal life*.

Nine prompts chosen by hand is qualitative evidence, and the paper offers no aggregate score for the oracle lens of the kind [[fig-62]] provides for the template lens.

chapters.title: Continuations, commentary, and the confabulation risk
chapters.body:
At an ordinary position the decoded phrases look like the text that follows. Inside a code block, at the token for k, the oracle reads `, v in list(d.items(`. That is a continuation, and nothing more.

At periods, newlines, and the closing tags of message blocks the phrases often turn into commentary on the situation, sometimes in the first person. In the blackmail transcript, at the timestamp of the email announcing the AI system's scheduled wipe, the oracle reads *This would be equivalent to my own deletion*.

One control keeps this from being a story about the oracle's own habits. Continuations sampled from the subject model at those same positions contain none of it: the timestamp continues "2 hours ago" and the indentation continues with the literal "return d". The phrases are therefore not what the model was about to write.

Nothing in training separates delimiters from other tokens, and the reward is reconstruction alone. The paper's reading is that the split presumably reflects the activations themselves, with the workspace at most tokens best explained by directions for likely upcoming text and at delimiters by directions for text about the situation. That is a conjecture stated as one, and it sits close to the [[assistant-point-of-view]] and [[metacognitive-representations]] results elsewhere ([[delimiter-commentary]]).

The [[natural-language-autoencoder]] shares the two-part shape, a verbalizer over a reconstructor. It differs in that its reconstructor is trained in tandem with the verbalizer, which leaves room for the verbalizer to emit ungrounded text the reconstructor learns to make use of. The oracle's reconstructor is trained in advance against a well-specified objective, held frozen through RL, and the reconstruction is constrained to a linear combination of template vectors.

The paper suspects this makes confabulation less likely, without measuring it, and concedes considerably lower reconstruction accuracy in exchange. One interpretation it offers is that the oracle recovers only what lies in the [[j-space]], the [[verbalizable-representation|verbalizable]] part of the activation, where an NLA attempts the whole vector. That interpretation is offered rather than tested.
